issues.legal_issue: Lands granted as remuneration for a village office belong to the office’s emoluments rather than to the officeholder’s family as divisible family property.
material_facts: Historical records and revenue proceedings described the lands as granted in lieu of remuneration for performing the village office.
The family’s own statements in the revenue proceedings treated the lands as emoluments for that office.
The office was held by family members in rotation, and a former officeholder retained the emoluments when it was another member’s turn to perform the duties.
The claimant was not the person performing the office when the revenue authorities made the impugned order.
issues.conclusion: The lands were service emoluments attached to the office, not family lands burdened with service; a family member who was not the officeholder had no right to a share in them.
issues.legal_principle: The 1859 Inam Rules, particularly Rules II, VI(2), VI(8), XIV(2) and XXI(2), do not give a non-serving family member a right to share service emoluments; Rule VI(2) concerns service that has been dispensed with or discontinued. Sections 3 and 9 of the Patels and Patwaris Law, 1900, provide for rotational office and enjoyment of the office’s emoluments by the person holding office. The distinction between a grant remunerating an office and a grant of land burdened with service is recognized in Lakhamgouda Basavaprabhu Sardesai v. Baswantrao; Venkata Jagannadha v. Veerabhadrayya is also discussed in relation to service lands.

predicates.civil_appeal_over_family_share_in_servic: The matter is a civil appeal concerning a family member’s claim to a share in lands associated with a village office.
predicates.historical_records_show_service_remunera: Records and statements by members of the family described the lands as remuneration for performing the village office.
predicates.claimant_is_not_current_officeholder: The family member claiming a share was not the person then holding and performing the village office.

issues.definition: When a civil appeal concerns a family member’s share in lands shown by historical records to remunerate a village office, and that claimant is not the current officeholder, the non-officiating family member has no share in the office’s emoluments.

issues.legal_issue: Revenue authorities may resume and regrant service lands when the person claiming them is not entitled to hold the service emoluments and the lands are administered as attached to the office.
material_facts: The revenue authorities determined that the person performing the village office was entitled to its emoluments and that the claimant was not entitled to retain the lands.
The claimant possessed the lands after a family partition but did not perform the office when the authorities ordered resumption and regrant.
The authorities ordered the lands resumed and regranted them to the person performing the office.
issues.conclusion: The revenue authorities had authority to resume the lands and regrant them to the working officeholder, and the orders were not invalid for want of jurisdiction.
issues.legal_principle: Section 190 of the Berar Land Revenue Code, 1928, permits forfeiture of alienated land granted on condition that services be rendered when the holder fails to render them or transfers the land in a way likely to defeat the grant’s purpose; forfeited land is regranted on the original conditions. Sections 9–11 of the Patels and Patwaris Law, 1900, regulate enjoyment and alienation of office emoluments. The court held that these provisions applied to the service grant at issue.

predicates.appeal_challenging_revenue_resumption: The matter is an appeal challenging a revenue authority’s resumption and regrant of lands.
predicates.lands_are_service_emoluments: The lands were granted as emoluments for performing the duties of an office.
predicates.claimant_does_not_perform_required_servi: The person claiming to retain the lands did not perform the service for which they were granted.
predicates.revenue_authority_regrants_to_working_of: The revenue authority regranted the lands to the person performing the office.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges resumption of lands that are service emoluments, the claimant does not perform the required service, and the authority regrants them to the working officeholder, the authority may resume and regrant the lands.

issues.legal_issue: A civil court cannot decide a claim to emoluments attached to a village office where the governing law assigns that matter to revenue authorities.
material_facts: The claimant brought a civil suit seeking possession and related relief on the basis that he had a share in lands treated as emoluments of a village office.
The governing provisions assigned decisions about office emoluments and related claims to revenue authorities.
issues.conclusion: The civil court had no jurisdiction to entertain a claim to a share in the office emoluments.
issues.legal_principle: Section 20 of the Patels and Patwaris Law, 1900, bars civil-court jurisdiction over claims to emoluments appertaining to the office of patel. Section 192 of the Berar Land Revenue Code, 1928, bars suits seeking decisions on matters that revenue authorities are empowered to determine, including claims against the State concerning property or emoluments of hereditary officers or servants.

predicates.civil_suit_claiming_share_in_office_emol: A person brought a civil suit claiming a share in emoluments attached to an office.
predicates.governing_law_assigns_emolument_claims_t: The applicable law assigns decisions about the office’s emoluments to revenue authorities.

issues.definition: When a civil suit claims a share in office emoluments and the governing law assigns such claims to revenue authorities, the civil court lacks jurisdiction over the claim.

issues.legal_issue: Plots previously recorded as part of a resumed estate remain service-grant lands when the authorities later exclude the entire service grant from resumption as a single unit.
material_facts: Two plots in the claimant’s possession had been recorded as revenue-paying land after they fell within a portion of the estate resumed from its holder.
A later government order excluded the patel’s lands from resumption and recorded them as his service grant, treating the lands as one homogeneous unit.
The claimant relied on earlier decrees concerning the plots, but those decrees related to other property.
issues.conclusion: The two plots remained part of the service grant and stood on the same footing as the other lands; they did not become the claimant’s private property.
issues.legal_principle: The 1922 government order excluded the service-grant lands from the estate-resumption proceedings as a whole and recorded them as the officeholder’s service grant. The court therefore treated the plots as part of that unit notwithstanding their earlier revenue classification. The applicable Inam Rules and service-grant provisions governed their character.

predicates.civil_appeal_claiming_specific_plots_as_: The matter is a civil appeal in which a claimant asserts that particular plots are private property rather than service-grant land.
predicates.later_order_treats_all_service_lands_as_: A later administrative order treats the officeholder’s lands as one service grant and excludes them from resumption as a unit.
predicates.earlier_decrees_do_not_cover_the_plots: The earlier court decrees relied on by the claimant concern property other than the particular plots.

issues.definition: When a civil appeal claims particular plots as private property, a later order treats all service lands as one grant, and the claimant’s earlier decrees do not cover those plots, the plots remain part of the service grant.

issues.legal_issue: Possession obtained through a family partition does not establish title by adverse possession against the government to lands held as emoluments of a village office.
material_facts: The claimant obtained possession of the lands through a family partition after a family member who had performed the office died.
The lands had been granted as emoluments for the office, and the claimant did not establish an independent right to a share in them.
The government later resumed the lands and regranted them to the person performing the office.
issues.conclusion: The claimant acquired no title by adverse possession against the government.
issues.legal_principle: Once the lands are found to have been granted as emoluments for an office, possession by a non-officiating family member does not establish a title by adverse possession against the government; the government may resume and regrant the service lands. The court relied on its characterization of the grant and the statutory regime governing service emoluments.

rule.if: civil_claim_based_on_adverse_possession and lands_are_service_emoluments and claimant_possesses_through_family_partition and claimant_has_no_right_to_the_emoluments

predicates.civil_claim_based_on_adverse_possession: The matter is a civil claim in which the claimant relies on adverse possession to establish title.
predicates.lands_are_service_emoluments: The lands were granted as emoluments for performing the duties of an office.
predicates.claimant_possesses_through_family_partit: The claimant obtained possession of the lands through a partition among family members.
predicates.claimant_has_no_right_to_the_emoluments: The claimant did not perform the office and had no independent right to its emoluments.

issues.definition: When a civil claim based on adverse possession concerns lands held as office emoluments, the claimant took possession through a family partition, and the claimant had no right to the emoluments, the claimant acquires no title by adverse possession against the government.
